The 'WS3-blocked coexistence read-order' test case (lines 188-193) specifies that the new XDG-cache path wins over a newer legacy file. This is correct for the migration window but the plan does not state what mechanism enforces XDG-wins-regardless-of-mtime in the storage primitive. The plan treats $XDG_CACHE_HOME as always writable after mkdir-p (lines 108-115), but does not address permission-failure handling at the storage primitive level. The cache-corruption-recovery test (lines 193-196) covers malformed JSON but not a directory that exists and is not writable (e.g. permission 555 set by an operator or by a container image). The risks section does not name this failure mode.

The segment-store retirement operation noted in the routed evidence section (lines 506-512) — 'design the segment store so that retirement is a first-class operation a curator pass can invoke' — is surfaced as a design note but not reflected in the WS2 acceptance criteria or the seen-state-storage module specification. The atomic temp+rename write contract for migration (lines 203-208) is correctly identified as critical and is covered by the race-safety test. However, the product-code step does not explicitly require atomic writes for routine (non-migration) watermark updates. If the storage primitive uses writeFile without atomic semantics for normal ticks, a crash mid-write produces a corrupted watermark that the cache-corruption-recovery path would then catch; this is acceptable but the design does not state the intent.

specialist_findings.claim: Pure-core / IO-at-the-edge layering is sound and fully specified. Tokenizer, ContextCostFileSystem, per-file computation, glob aggregation, and option parser are all pure-dependency-injected layers. Only file-system-node.ts and the topic handler in WS5 touch real IO, matching the stated principle. The composition root is a single explicit point (runContextCostCli), not scattered across layers.

Tokenizer interface is correctly positioned as a swap seam. Constructor-level substitution (chars/4 → tiktoken or Anthropic count_tokens) requires no cross-codebase refactor. The interface is minimal (one method: estimate(text: string) => number) and future implementations remain backward-compatible.

Error ownership is explicitly layered and documented. readFileUtf8/expandGlob propagate raw errors; tokenizeFile is the single re-throw boundary into ContextCostFileReadError; tokenizeGlobs lets glob-expansion errors propagate to the CLI exit-2 path. This is a well-defined error contract with no silent zeroing.

cwd resolution (D12) is deliberately caller-supplied rather than git-root-resolved. This is architecturally consistent with shell-tool convention, but means globs evaluated from a non-root invocation will silently miss files outside that subtree. The plan does not surface this as a risk or document a usage constraint in the help text (D8 only says 'File glob to include'). If agents invoke the tool from subdirectories, the behaviour may surprise without a documented caveat.

D9 wires the production node ContextCostFileSystem (file-system-node.ts) inside cli.ts at the composition root, but the integration test in WS5 also injects a fake for the read-failure case (test 7) and for the help short-circuit (test 4). This means cli.ts must accept an injectable fs parameter — yet D9 says cli.ts 'composes parser + production fs adapter'. If cli.ts hard-wires the production adapter, the integration tests that inject a fake adapter cannot exercise the composition root. The plan does not make the injection seam on cli.ts explicit.

text.length counts UTF-16 code units (D1), which double-counts Unicode supplementary-plane characters (e.g. emoji). For the current English-prose rule estate this is within the documented ±10-15% band, but the plan's accuracy claim is stated as a property of English-prose markdown only. If the rule/skill estate ever contains CJK text or emoji, the estimator silently degrades further without a corrective signal. The Tokenizer swap seam addresses this long-term, but no degradation signal or warning is specified.

Dependency choice (D10: tinyglobby) follows the build-vs-buy attestation protocol. The rejection of hand-rolling ** expansion is well-reasoned (cycle protection, symlink avoidance). The plan correctly restricts the real tinyglobby import to a single file (file-system-node.ts), so the vendor boundary is contained and replaceable.

The plan correctly defers JSONL session-log harvest (passive mode), smart presets, and real-tokenizer integration to explicit follow-up plans registered in the strategic source. Non-goals are complete and precise, preventing scope creep at implementation time.

The plan's reviewer scheduling assigns three distinct architecture experts (betty/fred/wilma) to different implementation phases (lines 301-308) without specifying how their findings are reconciled or whether a single architectural owner holds the cross-phase coherence. With three separate reviewers across disjoint phases, architectural drift between the driver shape (phase 2-3) and the reconcile shape (phase 4-5) is a real risk if no single reviewer holds the full picture.

The plan defers moving fitness-managed coordination surfaces (e.g. active-claims) out of git as a Future Enhancement (lines 963-966), noting this is the right escalation if multi-checkout collisions remain painful after the plan. However, the plan also implements a custom JSON deep-merge driver specifically for active-claims. If the external-store escalation is exercised later, the driver becomes dead infrastructure. The plan does not assess the likelihood of that escalation or whether investing in the driver is the right architectural trade-off given that risk.

The plan explicitly excludes custom merge drivers for curated rule lists (distilled.md, principles.md, directives) on the grounds that semantics require owner judgement (lines 248-251). This is architecturally sound and consistent with the no-silent-mutation invariant. The reconcile-over-driver routing for semantic shapes is a deliberate and well-reasoned constraint.
